title: Functions
description: Package code into reusable building blocks with parameters, return values and scope.

subLevels.title: Defining functions
subLevels.summary: Write your own reusable commands with def.

blocks.text: You already use functions: print(), input(), int() and range(). A function is a named block of code that does one job. Now you will write your own.

items: Write the code once, use it many times
Give a clear name to a piece of work
Keep long programs tidy and easier to fix

blocks.text: A function is a reusable, named set of instructions.

blocks.code:
def greet():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Welcome to PyPath")

greet()
greet()
blocks.output:
Hello!
Welcome to PyPath
Hello!
Welcome to PyPath
explanation: def starts a function definition. greet is its name.
The empty ( ) and the colon : are required.
The indented lines are the function's body.
greet() calls the function — each call runs the body once.

blocks.text: Python reads your file from top to bottom. Defining a function does not run it — it only remembers it. The body runs when you call it.

explanation: The call on line 1 happens before Python has read the def.
Python stops with a NameError.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Calling a function above its def. Always put the def first and the call below it.

questions.prompt: Which word starts a function definition?
questions.explanation: Python uses def. Other languages use words like function, which is why it's a common guess.
questions.hint: Look at the very first word of the greet example in this lesson.
optionFeedback: Right: Python starts every function definition with def.
function is used in some other languages, but Python uses a much shorter word.
func is not a Python keyword; Python uses def.
Close, but Python uses the short form def, not the full word define.

questions.explanation: The def is only remembered, not run. print("B") runs first, then show() prints A.
questions.hint: Remember that a def block is only remembered until the function is called.
optionFeedback: Right: the def is only remembered, so print("B") runs first and then show() prints A.
Defining show() does not run it, so A can't appear until show() is called below print("B").
show() is called on the last line, so A is printed too.
print("B") is outside the function and runs on its own, so B is printed as well.

options: Function names must be written in capitals
The colon : is missing at the end of the def line
questions.explanation: Like if and for, a def line ends with a colon. Lowercase names and an indented body are correct.
questions.hint: Compare the def line with the if and for lines you learned earlier.
optionFeedback: Function names are usually lowercase, like greet and say_hi; capitals are not required.
Right: a def line must end with a colon, like if and for lines.
The body of a function must be indented, just like the body of an if.
Python does not use semicolons at the end of def lines.

options: Nothing, the function is never called
questions.explanation: beep() is called three times and each call prints beep once.
questions.code:
def beep():
    print("beep")

beep()
beep()
beep()
questions.hint: Count how many times the function is called, not how many times it is defined.
optionFeedback: The function is called three times, and each call prints beep again.
beep() is a call, not text in quotes, so it runs the function instead of printing its name.
The three beep() lines below the def are calls, so the body does run.
Right: each of the three calls prints beep once.

questions.prompt: What happens when Python reads a def block?
options: It remembers the function but does not run its body yet
It deletes the function after one call
questions.explanation: The body only runs when the function is called. That's why you can define a function and use it many times later.
questions.hint: Think about the say_hi example that failed because it was called too early.
optionFeedback: The body only runs when you call the function, not when Python reads def.
Python prints nothing when it reads def; only print() inside a called function shows text.
Right: def stores the function so you can call it later, as many times as you like.
A function can be called many times, like greet() twice in the lesson; it is not removed.

subLevels.title: Parameters
subLevels.summary: Pass values into a function so it can work with them.

blocks.text: A parameter is a variable in the brackets of the def line. When you call the function, the value you pass is stored in it.

explanation: name is the parameter.
In the first call name is "Asha", in the second it's "Ravi".

blocks.text: Separate parameters with commas. Values are matched in order.

blocks.code:
def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

add(2, 3)
add(10, 5)
explanation: In add(2, 3), a is 2 and b is 3.
In add(10, 5), a is 10 and b is 5.

items: Parameter: the name in the def line, like pet
Argument: the actual value you pass in the call, like "Tom"
Arguments are matched to parameters by position

blocks.code:
def describe(pet, age):
    print(f"{pet} is {age} years old")

describe("Tom", 3)
describe(3, "Tom")
blocks.output:
Tom is 3 years old
3 is Tom years old
explanation: Swapping the arguments swaps the values.
Python doesn't know what you meant — order matters.

blocks.output: TypeError: square() missing 1 required positional argument: 'n'
explanation: square needs one value for n.
Calling it with empty brackets is an error.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Calling a function with fewer (or more) arguments than it has parameters.
Each parameter needs a value when the function is called.

questions.explanation: word holds "Hi", and + joins it with "!". The name word is not printed — its value is.
questions.hint: Replace the parameter with the value passed in the call, then do the joining.
optionFeedback: Right: word holds "Hi", and + joins it with "!".
word has no quotes inside the function, so its value is used, not the name.
The function adds "!" to the word before printing it.
Both values are strings, so + can join them without an error.

questions.prompt: In def area(width, height):, what are width and height?
questions.explanation: The names in the def line are parameters. Arguments are the values you pass when calling, like area(3, 4). The function's name is area, and area(3, 4) is a call.
questions.hint: Recall the difference between the names in the def line and the values in a call.
optionFeedback: Arguments are the actual values passed in a call, like area(3, 4).
Right: names inside the brackets of the def line are parameters.
The function's name is area; width and height are inside its brackets.
A call would look like area(3, 4); this line defines the function instead.

questions.explanation: a is 3 and b is 10 because arguments are matched in order, so a - b is -7.
questions.hint: Arguments are matched in order, so work out which value goes into a and b.
optionFeedback: 7 would be 10 - 3, but a is 3 and b is 10, so the answer is negative.
a - b is not in quotes, so Python works out the subtraction instead of printing the text.
Right: a is 3 and b is 10, so a - b is -7.
Subtracting a bigger number is allowed; it just gives a negative answer.

subLevels.title: Return values
subLevels.summary: Send a result back from a function with return.

blocks.text: return hands a value back to the code that called the function. You can store it in a variable.

blocks.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(4)
print(result)
explanation: double(4) works out 4 * 2.
return sends 8 back.
result stores the returned value.
square(3) returns 9 and square(4) returns 16.
You can use them in maths just like numbers: 9 + 16 = 25.

blocks.text: print shows a value on the screen. return gives it back to your code. They are not the same.

blocks.code:
def shown(n):
    print(n * 2)

def given(n):
    return n * 2

a = shown(5)
b = given(5)
print(a)
print(b)
explanation: shown(5) prints 10 but returns nothing.
A function without return gives back None, Python's "no value".
given(5) returns 10, so b holds 10.

blocks.text: If you need to use the result later, return it.

explanation: For 20, the first return runs and the function ends immediately.
For 12, the if is skipped and the second return runs.
a + b is worked out, then thrown away.
Nothing is returned, so the call gives None.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing the calculation but forgetting the word return. The function then gives back None.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Lines after a return inside the same block never run.

questions.explanation: x * 3 with x = 4 is 12, and return sends it back to print. 7 would be 4 + 3, which is not what * does.
questions.hint: Put 4 in place of x and work out what * does with it.
optionFeedback: 7 is 4 + 3, but * means multiply, not add.
Right: 4 * 3 is 12, and return sends it back to print.
x is the number 4, not text, so * multiplies instead of repeating.
The function has a return line, so it gives back a value instead of None.

questions.explanation: f prints 3 but has no return, so y is None. Both lines appear: first 3 from inside f, then None.
questions.code:
def f(x):
    print(x)

y = f(3)
print(y)
questions.hint: Think about what a function gives back when it has no return line.
optionFeedback: f prints 3, but it has no return, so y is None, not 3.
print(x) inside f still runs when f(3) is called, so 3 appears first.
3 is printed inside f, but there is a second print for y too.
Right: f prints 3, then returns None because it has no return line.

options: Prints the value on the screen for the user
Sends a value back to the code that called it and ends the function
Runs the function again from the very top
Saves the value so every function can use it
questions.explanation: return gives a value back to the code that called the function, and the function stops there. Showing it on screen is print's job, and return does not repeat the function.
questions.hint: Recall the print vs return page and what the variable b received.
optionFeedback: Showing a value on screen is print's job; return passes it back to your code.
Right: return hands the value back to the caller and the function stops there.
return ends the function; it never starts it again from the top.
return gives the value only to the code that called the function; it doesn't share it everywhere.

questions.prompt: This prints None instead of 10. What's the problem?
options: w and h must be named width and height
result must be printed inside the function
questions.explanation: result is calculated but not returned, so the call gives None. Adding return result fixes it.
questions.hint: Check whether result is ever handed back to the code that called area.
optionFeedback: Parameter names can be anything; w and h work fine.
print can show what a function returns, like print(square(3)) in the lesson.
Right: result is calculated but not returned, so the call gives back None.
Printing inside would show 10, but area(2, 5) would still return None for the outer print.

questions.explanation: -2 < 0 is True, so the first return runs and the function ends. The second return is never reached.
questions.hint: Check whether -2 < 0 is True, and remember what return does to the function.
optionFeedback: Right: -2 < 0 is True, so the first return runs and the function ends.
The second return is never reached, because the first return already ended the function.
return ends the function, so only one of the two returns can ever run.
Both paths have a return, so the function always gives back a word, never None.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so print(add(1, 2)) shows 3.
questions.explanation: return a + b sends 3 back to print. Using print inside would show 3 but then print(add(1, 2)) would also show None.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between showing a value and handing it back to the caller.
optionFeedback: Right: return a + b sends 3 back, and print shows it.
print would show 3 inside the function, but add would return None, so None is printed too.
give is not a Python keyword; the word that sends a value back is return.
result = a + b only stores the sum in a local variable, so the function still returns None.

subLevels.title: Default and keyword arguments
subLevels.summary: Give parameters default values and pass arguments by name.

blocks.text: A parameter can have a default value. If the caller leaves it out, the default is used.

blocks.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

greet("Asha")
greet("Ravi", "Welcome")
explanation: greeting="Hello" sets a default.
The first call doesn't pass a greeting, so "Hello" is used.
The second call passes "Welcome", which replaces the default.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Parameters with defaults must come after the ones without. def greet(greeting="Hello", name): is a SyntaxError.
You can pass an argument by naming its parameter: name=value. Then the order doesn't matter, and you can skip defaults you don't want to change.

blocks.code:
def order(item, size="medium", sugar=1):
    print(f"{size} {item}, sugar: {sugar}")

order("tea")
order("coffee", sugar=0)
order(size="large", item="juice")
blocks.output:
medium tea, sugar: 1
medium coffee, sugar: 0
large juice, sugar: 1
explanation: order("tea") uses both defaults.
sugar=0 changes only sugar; size keeps its default.
With keywords, item and size can be given in any order.

blocks.text: Defaults make arguments optional. Keywords make calls easier to read.

questions.explanation: times wasn't passed, so its default 2 is used and "ha" * 2 is "haha". No error, because the parameter has a default.
questions.hint: times was not passed in the call, so check the def line for its value.
optionFeedback: times defaults to 2, so the word is repeated twice, not shown once.
The default is 2, not 3, so "ha" is repeated only twice.
times has a default value, so leaving it out is allowed.
Right: the default times=2 is used, and "ha" * 2 is "haha".

questions.explanation: Keyword arguments are matched by name, not position, so name is "Mia" and age is 9.
questions.hint: Keyword arguments are matched by name, so check which value went to each name.
optionFeedback: With keyword arguments the order in the call doesn't matter; name is still "Mia".
Right: name="Mia" and age=9 are matched by name, so the f-string gives Mia-9.
The f-string shows the values in {name} and {age}, not the parameter names.
Passing arguments by name in any order is allowed, so there is no error.

questions.prompt: Which function definition causes a SyntaxError?
questions.explanation: A parameter without a default can't come after one with a default. The other three are all valid.
questions.hint: Recall the common mistake about where parameters with defaults must go.
optionFeedback: This is valid: the parameter with a default comes after the one without.
This is valid: every parameter has a default, so the order rule is never broken.
Right: b has no default but comes after a=1, which Python does not allow.
This is valid: two normal parameters with no defaults.

questions.prompt: When is a default value used?
options: When the caller doesn't pass a value for that parameter
Always, even when the caller passes a different value
Only when the function has no return line
Only when the call uses keyword arguments
questions.explanation: A passed value always replaces the default. The default only fills in when nothing is given, with or without keyword arguments.
questions.hint: Compare greet("Asha") with greet("Ravi", "Welcome") and look at the greetings.
optionFeedback: Right: the default only fills in when the caller leaves that argument out.
A value passed by the caller always replaces the default, as "Welcome" did.
Defaults have nothing to do with return; they are about missing arguments.
Defaults also work with normal calls, like order("tea") in the lesson.

subLevels.title: Scope
subLevels.summary: Learn where variables live: inside or outside a function.

blocks.text: A variable created inside a function is local: it only exists while the function runs. Outside the function, it's gone.

blocks.code:
def make_tea():
    cups = 2
    print(f"Making {cups} cups")

make_tea()
print(cups)
blocks.output:
Making 2 cups
NameError: name 'cups' is not defined
explanation: cups is created inside make_tea.
When the function ends, cups disappears.
The last line can't find it, so Python raises a NameError.

blocks.text: A variable created outside all functions is global. Functions can read it.

blocks.code:
shop = "PyCafe"

def welcome():
    print(f"Welcome to {shop}")

welcome()
explanation: shop is defined at the top level.
welcome() can read it without any extra work.

blocks.text: If you assign to a name inside a function, Python makes a new local variable — even if a global has the same name. The global is not changed.

blocks.code:
x = 10

def change():
    x = 99
    print(f"inside: {x}")

change()
print(f"outside: {x}")
explanation: x = 99 creates a local x inside change().
The global x is still 10.

blocks.text: Assigning inside a function creates a local variable.
The clean way for a function to change a value: take it as a parameter and return the new value. The caller decides where to store it.

blocks.code:
score = 10

def add_bonus(points):
    return points + 5

score = add_bonus(score)
print(score)
explanation: score is passed in as points.
The function returns 15.
The caller stores it back in score.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Expecting total = total + n inside a function to change a global total. Python treats total as local and raises an error. Pass it in and return it instead.

items: Local: made inside a function, lives only during the call
Each call gets fresh local variables

questions.explanation: y is local to f and disappears when f ends, so print(y) can't find it and Python raises a NameError. Calling f() first doesn't make y available outside, so it does not print 5.
questions.hint: Remember what happens to a variable made inside a function once the call ends.
optionFeedback: y only existed while f was running, so it's gone when print(y) runs.
Right: y is local to f, so print(y) outside can't find it and Python raises a NameError.
None is what a function returns without return; here the problem is that y doesn't exist outside.
A TypeError is about wrong arguments, like a missing one; a name that can't be found gives a different error.

questions.explanation: Functions can read global variables, so show() prints the global n.
questions.hint: Recall what a function may do with a variable created outside all functions.
optionFeedback: Right: show() can read the global n, so it prints 1.
n was created outside the function, and functions can read global variables, so there is no error.
show() prints the value of n; None would only appear if you printed what show() returns.
Nothing ever sets n to 0; it holds 1 from the first line.

questions.explanation: a = 7 inside set_a creates a new local a. The global a is untouched and is still 3.
questions.code:
a = 3

def set_a():
    a = 7

set_a()
print(a)
questions.hint: Assigning to a name inside a function creates a separate box for it.
optionFeedback: a = 7 inside set_a makes a new local a; the global a is not changed.
print(a) prints the global variable a, which holds a number, not None.
Right: the global a is untouched and still holds 3.
a was created at the top of the file, so print(a) can find it.

options: A variable that every function in the file can change
A variable created at the top of the file, outside functions
A variable made inside a function that exists only during the call
A variable whose value can never be changed
questions.explanation: Local means "belongs to this function call". A variable at the top of the file, outside all functions, is global.
questions.hint: Think about the make_tea example and where cups could be used.
optionFeedback: No function can change a local from another function; locals belong to one call only.
A variable made at the top of the file, outside all functions, is global, not local.
Right: a local variable is made inside a function and lives only during that call.
Local variables can be changed while the function runs; local is about where they live, not whether they change.

options: Each call of a function gets fresh local variables
Local variables keep their values between calls
A function can't read variables from outside
questions.explanation: Locals are created again on every call and thrown away at the end. Functions can read globals, and parameters are local.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to local variables when a call ends and a new one starts.
optionFeedback: Right: locals are made fresh on each call and thrown away when it ends.
Locals are thrown away when the call ends, so nothing is kept for the next call.
Functions can read global variables, like welcome() reading shop.
Parameters belong to the function call, so they are local, not global.

questions.prompt: Calling add(5) raises an error. What's the cleanest fix?
options: Call add(5) twice so that total exists first
Take total as a parameter and return total + n
Delete the line total = 0 at the top of the file
Add print(total) as the first line inside add
questions.explanation: Assigning total inside the function makes it local, so total + n has nothing to read yet. Passing total in and returning the new value (total = add(total, 5)) avoids the problem. Calling twice, deleting the global or printing it first still leaves total local, so the error stays.
questions.code:
total = 0

def add(n):
    total = total + n

add(5)
questions.hint: Remember the "Pass in, return out" page and how add_bonus changed score.
optionFeedback: Calling twice doesn't help: total is still local inside add, so the same error happens.
Right: pass total in and return total + n, then store the result outside.
Deleting the global doesn't fix it; total inside the function still has no value to read.
Printing total first still treats total as local, so it fails before anything is printed.

questions.explanation: c is a fresh local variable on every call: it starts at 0 and becomes 1. The first call's c doesn't carry over, so it's not 2.
questions.code:
def count():
    c = 0
    c += 1
    return c

count()
print(count())
questions.hint: Every call starts again from the first line of the function body.
optionFeedback: The first call's c is thrown away, so the second call starts again from 0.
c += 1 runs before return, so the function gives back 1, not 0.
count() has a return line, so print shows a number, not None.
Right: c is fresh on every call: it starts at 0 and becomes 1.

projects.title: Python Quiz Game
projects.summary: A three-question quiz with reusable ask() and grade() functions and a bonus question.

briefing.title: Build a Python Quiz Game
text: You'll write a small quiz. One function asks a question and returns the points earned, another turns the score into a rating.
The last question is a bonus worth 2 points, thanks to a default argument.
why: Writing a function once and calling it many times is how real programs stay short
It uses parameters, return values, default and keyword arguments
briefing.sampleOutput:
=== Python Quiz ===
What does print() do? (show/store) show
Correct!
Is 10 > 3 True? (yes/no) no
Not quite. The answer is yes.
Keyword to define a function? def
Correct!
You scored 3 out of 4.
Rating: Good effort

finalCode: score += ask("Keyword to define a function?", "def", points=2)

stages.instruction: ask() needs the question, the right answer and how many points it's worth. Most questions are worth 1 point.

question.explanation: Parameters with a default value go last (4.4).

optionFeedback: Parameters with a default value go last (4.4).
A parameter with a default can't come before ones without. This is a SyntaxError.
Without a default, every call would have to pass the points.
The colon at the end is missing. This is a SyntaxError.

stages.title: Ask the question
stages.instruction: Show the question with a space after it and keep what the player types.

question.explanation: + joins the question and a space into one prompt for input() (1.4).

optionFeedback: input() takes only one prompt. Two arguments is a TypeError.
print() shows the question but returns None, so nothing is typed.
The variable must be on the left of =. This is a SyntaxError.
+ joins the question and a space into one prompt for input() (1.4).

stages.title: Return the points
stages.instruction: If the reply matches the answer, say so and send the points back to whoever called ask().

question.prompt: Which line sends the points back?
question.explanation: return hands a value back to the caller, so score += ask(...) can add it (4.3).

optionFeedback: print shows the number but the function still returns None. score += None is a TypeError.
Always returning 1 ignores the bonus question's 2 points.
return hands a value back to the caller, so score += ask(...) can add it (4.3).
This returns the word points, and score += "points" is a TypeError.

stages.title: A wrong answer
stages.instruction: If the reply was wrong, show the right answer and return 0 points.

question.prompt: Why can these lines sit outside the if?
options: A right answer already left the function with return, so only wrong answers get here
Code after an if always runs before the if
Because answer is a global variable
question.explanation: return ends the function at once, so the lines after it only run for wrong answers (4.3).

optionFeedback: return ends the function at once, so the lines after it only run for wrong answers (4.3).
Code runs from top to bottom. The if comes first.
Only lines after a return that actually ran are skipped. A wrong answer never reaches it.
answer is a parameter of ask(), which makes it local (4.5).

stages.title: Work out a percentage
stages.instruction: grade() turns a score into a rating. First work out the score as a percentage of the total.

question.prompt: Which line works out the percentage?

optionFeedback: This gives 3 / 100 * 4 = 0.12, not a percentage.
Upside down: 4 * 100 / 3 is over 100%.
3 out of 4 is 3 * 100 / 4 = 75.0 percent (1.3).
total is a number, not a function. Calling it is a TypeError.

stages.title: Pick a rating
stages.instruction: Check the best rating first: 80% or more is a Python star, 50% or more is a good effort.

question.prompt: Which line should be checked first?
question.explanation: Check from the highest rule down; the first True return wins (2.3, 4.3).

optionFeedback: Checked first, 90% would also match >= 50 and get Good effort.
Check from the highest rule down; the first True return wins (2.3, 4.3).
Exactly 80% wouldn't count as a Python star.
The operator is >=, not =>. This is a SyntaxError.

stages.title: Play the quiz
stages.instruction: Start the score at 0, then ask three questions. The last is the bonus question worth 2 points.

question.prompt: Which line asks the bonus question?
options: score = ask("Keyword to define a function?", "def", points=2)
score += ask("Keyword to define a function?", "def", points=2)
score += ask("Keyword to define a function?", "def", 2 = points)
ask("Keyword to define a function?", "def", points=2)
question.explanation: points=2 is a keyword argument, and += adds the returned points to the score (4.4).

optionFeedback: = replaces the score, so the first two answers would be lost.
points=2 is a keyword argument, and += adds the returned points to the score (4.4).
Keyword arguments are name=value, not value=name. This is a SyntaxError.
The returned points are thrown away, so the score doesn't change.

stages.title: Show the result
stages.instruction: Print the score, then call grade() inside an f-string to show the rating.

question.explanation: You can call a function inside the braces of an f-string; its return value is shown (4.3).

optionFeedback: Without brackets the function isn't called; Python shows <function grade ...>.
Arguments are matched in order, so score and total would be swapped.
Without the f, the braces are printed as plain text.
You can call a function inside the braces of an f-string; its return value is shown (4.3).

walkthrough: ask() shows a question, compares the reply and returns the points or 0.
points=1 is a default, so only the bonus question passes points=2.
grade() checks from the highest rating down and returns the first that matches.
score lives outside the functions; each score += ask(...) adds the returned points.
3 out of 4 is 75%, which is a Good effort.

cheatSheet.title: Functions

items.note: Define once with def, call as often as you like.
Parameters take values in; return sends a result back.

items.code:
def show(x):
    print(x)

result = show(1)
print(result)
items.note: Without return, a function gives back None.

items.code:
def hello(name, greeting="Hi"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}"

print(hello("Ravi"))
print(hello("Ravi", greeting="Hey"))
items.note: Defaults go last; keyword arguments name the parameter.

items.code:
def f():
    x = 1
    return x

print(f())
items.note: Variables made inside a function are local to it.

items.code:
rate = 2
def double(n):
    return n * rate

print(double(5))
items.note: A function can read global variables.

remember: Define a function before you call it.
print shows a value; return hands it back.
